paragraphs.heading: A twist instead of a push
paragraphs.text: Torque is the turning partner of ordinary force. A force is a push or a pull on a body; torque is a twist applied to an object about a chosen axis. It also goes by the names moment of force, or just moment. When you drive a screw, the screwdriver puts torque on the screw, so the screw tends to turn around its axis.

paragraphs.heading: Names and symbols
paragraphs.text: Which word people use depends on place and field. Physicists tend to say torque, while engineers tend to say moment. In British and American mechanical engineering, the usual term is moment of force, shortened to moment, a usage that goes back at least to 1811 in Siméon Denis Poisson's Traité de mécanique. An English version of that book came out in 1842. In equations torque is usually written with the Greek letter tau (𝜏), and as moment of force it is often written M.

paragraphs.heading: How big a twist is
paragraphs.text: To find the torque about an axis, take the part of the force that pushes at right angles to a lever and multiply it by how far from the pivot, or fulcrum, it acts. That distance is called the lever arm. Put more exactly, torque is the size of the perpendicular part of the force times the distance from the force's line of action to the point being considered. Formulas for it use θ, the angle that the force makes with the lever arm. Torque is measured in newton-metres, written N⋅m.

paragraphs.heading: Torque changes spin
paragraphs.text: The torque on a particle equals how fast its angular momentum changes with time. With several forces, Newton's second law gives d𝐋/dt = 𝐫 × 𝐅ₙₑₜ = 𝝉ₙₑₜ. The same idea extends to a group of particles by adding them up, and to a solid mass by integrating over every point in it. The principle of moments, or Varignon's theorem, adds that the combined torque from many forces about a point is the sum of each one's torque.

paragraphs.heading: Torque and power
paragraphs.text: Torque also links to power. The power a torque delivers depends only on how fast the object is turning at that instant. It does not matter whether the spin is speeding up, slowing down or steady. The same relation can be turned around to work out the torque from a given turning speed and power output.

paragraphs.heading: Not the same as energy
paragraphs.text: The newton-metre has the same dimensions as the joule, yet the joule is not used for torque. Strictly, torque could be given in N⋅m per radian, since it is the rate at which work changes as the angle changes. But SI treats the radian as having no dimension, so torque is simply written in N⋅m. Torque is also a vector, pointing in three-dimensional space, while energy is a scalar. For both reasons, sharing a unit does not make torque and energy the same quantity.

paragraphs.heading: Older units
paragraphs.text: The traditional imperial units are the pound foot and, for small amounts, the pound inch. In the United States people usually say foot-pound and inch-pound. Readers rely on context and the hyphen to tell that these mean torque and not energy.
